stories.headline: Man City cheated because Premier League was built to be unfair
stories.summary: The Premier League is unfair: Some teams are allowed to spend more than everyone else. So, of course Man City cheated to win.
stories.body:
Back in 1887, everyone was already playing soccer, or football, in England. The Premier League didn't exist -- nor did any other league. Instead, there was the Birmingham Cup, the Staffordshire Cup, the Lancashire Cup, the English Cup, the Welsh Cup, the FA Cup, and plenty of other tournaments that were seemingly being created at random every other day.

The problem with the ad-hoc, knockout-only schedule is that, as the founder of the Football League William McGregor put it, there was no "fixity of fixtures." Teams would get knocked out of multiple tournaments early and have nowhere to play. Or they'd make a deep run in the FA Cup and have to cancel their games in Lancashire Cup because, how were they supposed to know they'd make it to the semifinals of the FA Cup?

Fans didn't love it either. McGregor said "became disgusted by the intermittent fare provided for them."

Born in Scotland, McGregor emigrated to Birmingham around 1870. He owned a small drapery shop and eventually became an administrator for one of the leading, nascent football clubs in the area: Aston Villa.

"A great many people saw the difficulty which football and footballers were in; I happened, luckily, to be the one man at that particular time who saw the way out," he said, according to The Story of Association Football, written by J.A.H. Catton in 1926. "It appeared to me that a fixed program of home-and-home matches between the leading clubs in the country ... would produce football of a more interesting nature than the average game we saw."

In March of 1888, McGregor suggested to five of the other leading clubs in England that they form a 12-team competition with this "fixity of fixtures." By September, the Football League played its first matches.

Historians initially suggested that McGregor came up with the idea of a "league" from cricket, the country's other most-popular sport. However, as shown by Andrew Zimbalist and Stefan Szymanski, authors of "National Pastime: How Americans Play Baseball and the Rest of the World Plays Soccer," it seems more likely that McGregor was inspired by the success of baseball's National League over in the United States.

But the inspiration ended with the schedule. The National League was a closed system where the owners would only welcome new clubs if they all thought it would increase everyone's profits. Sport and business were tied together from the start.

Instead, the Football League accepted its place within the Football Association, England's larger governing body for the sport. From day one, league rules included language about the worst-performing teams being replaced by the best-performing teams from a lower league. The FA imposed a rule that no team directors could be paid for their services.

In contrast to the front-and-center business interests of the National League, McGregor envisioned the Football League as an organization founded on "the joint principles of self-interest and mutual advantage." He proposed that the attendance revenue from matches -- at the time, the only source of revenue -- be shared equally by the hosts and the visitors.

With the home-and-away fixtures and the promotion-and-relegation structure eventually adopted by the majority of sports leagues created across the world over the next 100 years, it's not inconceivable that everyone would've adopted this principle of financial equality, too. But instead, 10 of the 12 Football League clubs voted McGregor's proposal down.

All of which, eventually, led us to where Manchester City and the Premier League are today: an English club that is essentially owned by a trillion-dollar sovereign wealth fund from a natural-resource-rich Middle Eastern nation is facing expulsion from the league that McGregor created because those owners artificially inflated their revenues by more than $1 billion so they could compete with the biggest teams in a competition that now makes close to $10 billion a year.

In short, it led to a scenario in which Manchester City cheated the financial rules because, well, they kind of had to if they wanted to win a Premier League title.

Which is more competitive: The NFL or the Premier League?
There are lots of inherent contradictions in the way we decide to determine our champions.

By some definitions, American sports are way more competitive than European soccer. Six different teams have won the last 10 NFL titles, nine teams have won the last 10 NBA championships, and seven different sides have won the last 10 World Series.

These leagues have salary caps and tax penalties to prevent any team from spending too much money, and they all seek to increase parity by allowing the worst teams in the leagues every season to hire the best amateur players in the world through their annual drafts.

But to an economist, American sports leagues are the exact opposite of competitive: they're monopolies or cartels. There's no real punishment for losing -- if anything, you're rewarded for losing. And new teams can only be added to the existing leagues if the other owners agree to let them in and if the new owners agree to pay billions of dollars in fees to join.

European sport, in turn, is as competitive as it gets -- at least, from the economist's point of view. You win the league by winning the most matches across the same exact schedule of games as everyone else in the league. If you finish too low, you get dropped down to a lower league. Win enough games in that lower league? You get rewarded by promotion to a more prestigious competition.

The advantages to this approach are clear. Anyone can, theoretically, create a team and get promoted up the pyramid. So, there are soccer clubs just about everywhere in England. While fewer than half of the states in the U.S. have an NFL team because of the closed structure, there are 17 professional soccer teams in London alone.

Fans benefit with more access to attending games at home this way, and they also benefit by not having to sit through uncompetitive matches where both teams are actively trying to lose and jockeying for a higher draft pick.

The structure seems to serve the players, too. While contracts for the best soccer players pale in comparison to the major American sports, the player pool is so much bigger across the wider soccer economy. On top of that, Premier League clubs, on average, put 66% of their revenues back into player wages. Across American sports, teams only spend about 50% of revenue on salaries.

Of course, if baseball players are making way more money than soccer players despite getting a smaller chink of the pie, then it's clear which structure is better for business: the one where everyone gets to stay in the league no matter how bad they are. It aligns the interests of owners and makes revenues way more consistent, year after year.

The problem with professional soccer -- the issue that's constantly pulling at the core of the idea, the thing that McGregor seemed worried about 150 years ago -- is that the structure only remains fair and truly competitive when the financial resources of the competitors remain somewhat equal.

Without those guardrails in place, the economy of the world's most popular sport eventually came to mirror the economy at large: those with initial, inherent structural advantages kept winning, while everyone else floundered about in varying degrees of precarity.

It's no coincidence, then, that of five Premier League clubs to win multiple Premier League titles, four have never been relegated. It's also no coincidence that the fifth one -- the only team to be relegated at some point and win more than one Premier League title -- is Manchester City.

Why the Premier League was unfair even before Man City were found guilty
When every game matters and everyone else is spending as much as they can, what are you, the wealthy owner of a mid-table club, going to do?

A small-market billionaire owner in Major League Baseball can hide behind the notion that they can't spend more money since there's no punishment for cutting costs and winning fewer games.

A Premier League owner could try to devote less of their revenues to wages in order to post a higher annual profit -- but then they risk getting relegated, which both craters revenues and tanks the team's valuation if you wanted to try to sell the club. That means even less money available to go to wages next year.

Club directors weren't even allowed to take salaries until 1982, when suddenly the sport became a big, global business. The boom came with the expansion of the UEFA Champions League beyond just, you know, league champions throughout Europe, along with the rapid expansion of broadcast technology at the beginning of the 1990s and the Premier League breaking away from the Football League to form England's top-flight league.

In a way, the open structure of the sport was such a bad business idea -- everyone spends all of their money; nobody knows what their profits will be in a year, let alone three -- that it was actually a good business idea. It led to the proliferation of teams across England, which led to a generational, emotional connection between fans and club.

The open structure meant every game mattered. The stakes combined with the impossible-to-fake atmosphere created by the generations of local fans made for a great television product. That TV product made lots of money, and that, in turn, made the stakes of every game, literally, worth even more.

The potential revenues on offer from being in the Premier League or competing in the Champions League were so great that so many clubs were willing to push themselves to the financial brink in order to shoot the moon, have that one great season, and establish themselves in a new financial tier. By 2011, according to UEFA, all of the first-division clubs on the continent had combined for a profit of ... just kidding. The clubs combined for losses worth a total of €1.67 billion.

Now "rich owners losing money to make their soccer teams better" isn't a pressing societal problem. But unlike in American sports, where teams are franchises and so the money the New York Jets spend is the same as the money the New York Jets owner spends, soccer owners who spent on their teams were actually loaning the money to what were still viewed as something closer to local institutions. So, all of that debt was, technically, money that these important institutions owed to their rich owners.

This was, theoretically, one of two reasons why UEFA introduced "Financial Fair Play," which essentially limited the losses a club could post to a preset amount. All of the other financial regulations that have come since FFP are some version of the same idea: limiting spending based on how much revenue the club brings in.

Theoretically, FFP was successful. In 2017, first-division clubs posted over €1 billion in profits. After a couple years of reversion due to COVID-19, profits and losses were essentially even for the last financial year. The first-division clubs of Europe are expected to turn a profit whenever the next set of numbers are posted.

How much of this is due to FFP is unclear. A recent meta-analysis of various FFP studies found that the legislation did improve the profitability of clubs but that it had no effect on the actual indebtedness of teams. This is mostly due to how transfer fees are accounted for: as immediate lump-sum profit for the "selling" team but spread out across the years of the player's contract for the "buying" team.

Other studies determined that rising broadcast revenues of the past 20 years explain the improved financial performance as much as, if not more than, the new financial controls.

But while there is at least some evidence of FFP making clubs more sustainable, there is no evidence of it making the sport more "fair." If anything, there is evidence that it's done the exact opposite.

A recent study of 24 first-division leagues in Europe from researches at Sheffield Hallam University found the following over the 20-year period after FFP was introduced: "Seven of the 24 leagues examined have seen a statistically significant worsening of league concentration post-FFP, 14 leagues experienced a decline in the number of top-four finishers and 13 saw a reduction in the number of unique title winners. The weight of evidence indicates that FFP has adversely affected competitive balance in several European football leagues."

And, well, of course this happened. By limiting clubs to spend roughly how much they make, you are locking in the biggest and richest clubs as the best clubs.

It's no coincidence that these rules happened when they did, either. Right after the turn of the century, Russian oligarch Roman Abramovich turned Chelsea into one of the richest clubs in the world by spending billions of dollars of his own money before the FFP regulations were in place. Abu Dhabi United Group bought Manchester City in 2008. And Qatari Sports Investments bought Paris Saint-Germain in 2011.

If Abramovich-style spending was allowed to continue, then the owners of Liverpool, Arsenal, and Manchester United would've had to spend even more of their money to keep up -- especially if other oligarchs or sovereign-wealth funds or, god forbid, tech billionaires bought their own clubs. Instead, FFP told the owners of the biggest clubs in the world that they could spend less money without risking their place atop the global hierarchy since everyone else was told they had to spend even less.

The main difference between Chelsea and Man City is that Chelsea spent most of their money before the FFP regulations were in place. They did keep spending after the regulations were established, but since Abramovich was forced to sell the club in May 2022 after Russia's invasion of Ukraine and the new owners self-reported the various violations they uncovered, they were only punished with a fine.

Manchester City, of course, spent around $1 billion extra after the regulations were in place. They cheated the rules 114 different times. They lied to the league. They hindered the investigation. They created fraudulent accounting on a barely-believable scale.

Other clubs, like Newcastle and Aston Villa, have clearly wanted to spend more money than financial regulations have allowed them to, but rather than creating their own "sham" contracts, they were forced to dismantle their entire rosters and totally rebuild Champions League-level and trophy-winning teams. Man City must be punished, severely, to uphold some semblance of integrity under the current regulatory regime.

And by no means should we look at Abramovich, or QSI, or the UAE as heroes of this story. If we did, then the logical endpoint is ... what? Every team should be a sports-washing vehicle of someone or some country who is trying to find a new way to influence the various levers of the global economy?

Instead, what the Manchester City scandal hopefully, eventually, makes clear is just how unfair this sport is -- even when someone isn't illegally spending billions of dollars to build the best team that English soccer has ever seen.

Because when Arsenal won the title last year or Liverpool the year before or Manchester United (back when they used to win titles too), the main reason isn't that they're smarter, that they have the most passionate fans, or that their club has something that makes it inherently better than everyone else's.

No, the main reason they've won -- and will keep winning in the future -- is that the rules let them spend more money than everybody else.

stories.headline: How Kimi Antonelli can win F1 title at United States GP -- with or without Qatar, Abu Dhabi races
stories.summary: Kimi Antonelli took another big step towards his first world title after outscoring his two closest championship rivals, George Russell and Lewis Hamilton, at the Singapore Grand Prix.
stories.body:
Kimi Antonelli took another big step towards his first world title after outscoring his two closest championship rivals, George Russell and Lewis Hamilton, at the Singapore Grand Prix.

The 20-year-old, who has the potential to set a new record for the youngest Formula 1 champion this year, now leads Mercedes teammate Russell by 102 points in the standings with a maximum of 150 points still up for grabs.

The substantial lead means he could be crowned champion as early as Oct. 24 at the U.S. Grand Prix in Austin, but the maths around that calculation are slightly complicated by question marks over the final two races of the season. The grands prix in Qatar and Abu Dhabi are currently scheduled to go ahead on Nov. 29 and Dec. 6, but escalations in the war between the United States and Iran have the potential to force the cancellation of both rounds.

F1 has put a contingency plan in place to hold a single round at Imola if Qatar and Abu Dhabi are cancelled, but doing so would cut the championship short by one round and mean only 125 points are available to any single driver before the end of the year. Such a scenario would change the maths around the championship fight, making it easier for Antonelli to be crowned champion in Austin.

- 'Chucky' Verstappen is back. Luckily for Antonelli, it's too late

- Verstappen takes back-to-back wins with dominant Singapore drive

- Hamilton calls Singapore strategy 'painful lesson' after Ferrari apology

Alongside Russell and Hamilton, Max Verstappen, Charles Leclerc and Lando Norris are still mathematically in contention for this year's championship, although the incredibly slim hopes of Leclerc and Norris would be snuffed out entirely by the cancellation of the races in the Middle East.

What does Antonelli need to do to be crowned champion in Austin?
Assuming the final two races go ahead as planned, Antonelli's chances of clinching the title in Austin remain relatively slim. The Mercedes driver would need to win in Texas, with his teammate Russell finishing ninth or lower and Hamilton finishing fifth or lower.

Such a scenario would put Antonelli 125 points ahead of Russell with 125 points remaining, but even if Antonelli failed to score another point and Russell won all the remaining rounds after Austin, Antonelli would still be crowned champion on countback of race victories (by that stage Antonelli would be on nine and Russell on three with five races remaining).

If the championship is shortened by the season ending in Imola rather than Abu Dhabi, Antonelli would only need to leave Austin with a lead of 100 points over his rivals.

Such a scenario would result in the following permutations:

If Antonelli wins in Austin he would be crowned champion regardless of where the others finish.
If Antonelli finishes second, he would be crowned champion if Russell doesn't win the race.
If Antonelli finishes third, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes off the podium.
If Antonelli finishes fourth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes behind him and Hamilton does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes fifth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes fourth or lower and Hamilton does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes sixth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes fifth or lower and Hamilton does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes seventh, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes sixth or lower and Hamilton does not finish in the top two.
If Antonelli finishes eighth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes seventh or lower, Hamilton does not finish in the top two and Verstappen does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes ninth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes eighth or lower, Hamilton does not finish in the top three and Verstappen does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes tenth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes ninth or lower, Hamilton does not finish in the top three and Verstappen does not win the race.
If Antonelli fails to score, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes ninth or lower, Hamilton finishes fifth or lower and Verstappen does not win the race.

What's the minimum Antonelli needs to do be crowned champion?
Another way to look at the championship is the minimum amount of points Antonelli needs to score over the remaining rounds to secure the title regardless of what other drivers achieve. Assuming Qatar and Abu Dhabi go ahead, he needs 49 points over the remaining rounds, which could be achieved with as little as five sixth place finishes and one fifth place finish over the rest of the season.

If only five races remain, Antonelli would need just 24 points to secure the title, which would be attainable with two seventh place finishes and three eighth place finishes at the remaining rounds.

stories.headline: 'Hesitant' Valkyries lament their poor ball security in Game 2 loss to Dream
stories.summary: Golden State's miscues piled up on Monday night, and Atlanta kept capitalizing, scoring 24 points off 19 turnovers in the Dream's 79-65 victory over the Valkyries in Game 2 of the WNBA Finals, a decision that evened the best-of-seven series at 1-all.
stories.body:
SAN FRANCISCO -- Angel Reese stole the ball from Kaila Charles and began dribbling when Tiffany Hayes tried to regain possession, fouled the Atlanta center and sent her to the floor. The Dream star repeatedly slapped her right hand on the court, finding yet another way to fire up her team.

Golden State's miscues kept coming, and Atlanta kept capitalizing -- scoring 24 points off 19 turnovers to beat the Valkyries 79-65 in Game 2 of the WNBA Finals on Monday night and even the best-of-seven series at 1-all as it shifts to Atlanta.

"I think we were just a little too loose with the ball," Valkyries point guard Veronica Burton said. "Obviously that's what they're known for, and we're known for the opposite. It starts with me. I can't just be throwing the ball. It's one of the most important things is taking care of it and so I think just being organized, all being on the same page and then in fast break not getting too sped up, being decisive. I think we had a lot of times where we were hesitant or we weren't on the same page and that's where it led to turnovers."

Four of the five Golden State starters had two or more turnovers, with Kayla Thornton the only starter without one.

Rhyne Howard set a WNBA Finals single-game record with six steals, and DeWanna Bonner chipped in four more off the bench. Reese finished with 30 points and 16 rebounds.

Burton thought her team was outhustled by the determined Dream, who head home for Game 3 on Wednesday night. She committed three turnovers.

"You could tell that they ramped up their defense, so we've just got to stay focused, stay locked in," Golden State center Kiah Stokes said.

Valkyries coach Natalie Nakase credited the Dream for "their effort, their hustle, their fight," sprinting back on defense, getting their hands up and clogging the driving lanes.

"It's frustrating, that's been part of our identity. Because our identity is defense, we hang our hats on that," Nakase said. "The hustle is the turnovers because in order for you to get turnovers they have to kind of outhustle you to create the turnovers."

The Dream had just eight points off turnovers in their 68-64 Game 1 loss, then two days later returned to the defensive formula that got them this far. And that was crucial in tying up the series.

Nakase plans some conversations about sticking with a game plan and being organized on offense.

Burton will challenge herself to lead the way in taking better care of the ball.

"It starts with me. I've got to clean that up," she said, "and that's what we'll do."

stories.headline: 49ers hold off furious Commanders' second-half rally to go 6-0
stories.summary: The 49ers dominated in the first half but had to hold off a second-half Commanders rally.
stories.body:
SANTA CLARA, Calif. -- For about 30 minutes Monday night, the San Francisco 49ers looked poised to roll to their sixth consecutive victory against the Washington Commanders.

Then, wide receiver Mike Evans, attempting to play through a sore right Achilles, went down after a 16-yard catch. When he finally got back up moments later, he hobbled to the locker room and did not return.

Upon his departure, he took San Francisco's momentum with him. That left the Niners doing something they haven't had to do much of this season: scrambling to pull out a late victory.

Washington battled back from a 20-point deficit in a second half that almost flipped the script. Costly 49ers penalties paired with Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels' second-half rhythm, allowed Washington to come to within inches of taking a late lead and the upset.

Instead, safety Malik Mustapha's fourth-down pass breakup at the goal line paired with a clinching sack by Romello Height and Keion White spurred the Niners to a 23-17 win.

Though the Niners escaped with a win, the question now centers on Evans' health. San Francisco coach Kyle Shanahan said after the game that Evans' Achilles injury is the same thing (soreness) he dealt with all week. Shanahan said he didn't think Evans would need further testing or imaging.

The 49ers are already without wideouts Ricky Pearsall (knee), De'Zhaun Stribling (ankle), Demarcus Robinson (ankle), Deebo Samuel Sr. (hamstring) and Christian Kirk (calf), leaving quarterback Brock Purdy to throw to a patchwork group of receivers that includes Brandin Cooks, Jordan Watkins and Jacob Cowing. 49ers WRs not named Evans had two catches for 35 yards.

Although Kirk and Robinson are close to returning, the Niners might need to consider a trade to get some help.

Here are the most important things to know for both teams:

San Francisco 49ers (6-0)
What to make of Brock Purdy's performance: After five pass attempts on the game's opening drive, Purdy reached 1,500 career passes, which made him the highest-rated passer among qualified quarterbacks in league history. Purdy and the offense came out throwing and were on track for one of his biggest statistical performances of the season before a big lead and the injury to Evans left the Niners looking to run the ball and the clock to put away the game. Still, Purdy did more than his share in leading San Francisco to the win, finishing 21-of-29 for 264 yards and one touchdown. He didn't throw an interception and gained 28 yards on five carries.

Stat to know: Through the first five weeks, running back Christian McCaffrey was averaging his lowest number of touches (16) and scrimmage yards per game (84.6) since his rookie season in 2017. That has partially been by design to help McCaffrey stay fresh, but with Evans out, the Niners needed him Monday night. McCaffrey had his most active night of the season, finishing with 25 touches for 117 scrimmage yards and two touchdowns. He also lost a fumble as San Francisco was driving deep in Washington territory.

Trend to watch: With the exception of punter Corliss Waitman's continued excellence, the Niners special teams remained an adventure. For the second week in a row, returner Jacob Cowing muffed a punt, this time inside San Francisco's 5. He recovered it, but the Niners had to begin their least effective drive of the first half from the 4. What's more, kicker Eddy Pineiro missed his third extra point attempt of the season. That goes with his three missed field goal attempts to bring his total missed kicks for the season to six. That's the most in the NFL and more than he had all of last season. The Niners also were called for fair-catch interference on a punt that set up the Commanders at their 46 with 52 seconds left. For a team that has been so good on offense and defense, special teams are again emerging as a concerning question. -- Nick Wagoner

Next game: at Atlanta Falcons (Sunday, 1 p.m. ET)

Washington Commanders (1-4-1)
The Commanders were headed to an embarrassing defeat with a first half that did nothing to quell speculation on coach Dan Quinn's future -- especially after their overtime gaffe the previous week in a tie against the New York Giants. Washington needs to be beyond moral victories in Quinn's third season, but by rallying with a chance to win the game, the Commanders at least showed they could and would compete.

Even though multiple ownership sources said Quinn's job was safe, the rally certainly helped quiet that noise. If the Commanders play in the NFC East the way they did in the second half -- especially with how quarterback Jayden Daniels has played the past two weeks -- they can have a chance. Multiple team officials pointed out before the game that, regardless of Monday's outcome, they knew the season was far from over because of the NFC East's lackluster play. First up after the bye: a home game vs. the Philadelphia Eagles. The NFC East became the first division in NFL history to go winless in consecutive weeks in which all teams in the division played a game.

What to make of Jayden Daniels' performance: Daniels had one bad play in the first half when, on a fourth down, he threw the ball away. Quinn said he knew it was fourth down. He said someone asked him on the headset about the illegal shift on the play. Quinn told them they couldn't now kick a field goal. But other than that, Daniels played another solid game in rallying the Commanders from a 20-3 halftime deficit. Washington lacked a running game so the burden was on Daniels to produce. He threw two touchdown passes in the second half. Perhaps his best throw came on a third-and-8 with pressure in his face as he had to throw early to receiver Antonio Williams. The 23-yard completion and roughing penalty set up his second touchdown pass. Daniels completed 29 of 40 attempts for 300 yards.

Trend to watch: Red zone defense. It has been terrible for Washington as it given up 12 touchdowns in a row on red zone trips. It had given up nine straight entering the game and the 49ers scored a touchdown on their first three trips. The Commanders finally broke the streak by forcing a field goal late in the first half. They have struggled to defend tight ends in this area and, predictably, George Kittle caught the first touchdown pass of the game against zone coverage.

Most surprising performance: The Commanders' second-half defense. They had given up a combined 85 points in the past four second halves. They appeared to save their worst half for the first two quarters Monday by giving up 303 yards and 20 points. But in the second half, they gave up only 64 yards and three points, putting the offense in position to rally. Washington gave up 7.4 yards per play in the first half and 3.79 in the second half. -- John Keim

stories.headline: Griezmann has 2 goals, 1 assist for Orlando City in 4-1 win over DC United
stories.summary: Antoine Griezmann had two goals and an assist, Martín Ojeda added a goal and an assist, and Orlando City beat D.C. United 3-1 on Saturday night.
stories.body:
ORLANDO, Fla. -- - Antoine Griezmann had two goals and an assist, Martín Ojeda added a goal and an assist, and Orlando City beat D.C. United 3-1 on Saturday night.

Griezmann has 12 goals and seven assists in 14 MLS appearances and is the first player in league history with a goal contribution in 12 of his first 14 career games.

Marco Pasalić scored a stoppage-time goal for Orlando (12-13-5). Maxime Crépeau had three saves.

Tai Baribo converted from the penalty spot in first-half stoppage time for D.C. (7-10-12).

Ojeda, just inside the top of the 18-yard box, chipped a first-touch pass over four defenders to a charging Griezmann on the give-and-go for a first-touch finish from 7 yards out to make it 1-0 in the 15th minute.

Ojeda flicked a back-heel volley, off a feed from Griezmann, past goalkeeper Sean Johnson and inside the left post to give Orlando a two-goal lead in the 22nd.

Griezmann intercepted a misplayed pass by Kye Rowles in D.C.'s defensive third, took two dribbles and rolled a shot into the net to make it 3-1 in the 50th minute.

Johnson finished with three saves.

Up next D.C.: Plays Wednesday at Cincinnati.

Orlando: Hosts New York City next Saturday.

stories.headline: PSG match a test to show what Barcelona can do - Hansi Flick
stories.summary: Barcelona coach Hansi Flick challenged his players to show they can compete with Europe's best by beating PSG on Tuesday.
stories.body:
Barcelona coach Hansi Flick challenged his players to show they can compete with Europe's best by beating Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League on Tuesday to extend their perfect start to the season.

Barça have won 11 matches in a row to kick off the new campaign, scoring 48 goals in the process, but that streak will be put to the test by back-to-back European champions PSG at the Parc des Princes.

Both teams have won their opening two games in the Champions League, although PSG's 4-2 win at Manchester City last week demonstrated they are still the team to beat in Europe.

"It will be a good test for us to show how far we are," Flick said in the pre-game news conference on Monday.

"I would like my team to play with confidence, play brave and, of course, play together as a team. We did it in the last 11 games; now we play against, if you see the last two years, the best team in the world.

"For us, it's a good opportunity to show our level, show what we can do and [see] what we have to improve. After this match, we will also know a lot of things."

The two teams met in the league phase last season, with PSG running out 2-1 winners in Barcelona.

Flick acknowledges the French champions remain the more mature side, but feels Barça, who have not won the Champions League since 2015, pose a completely different proposition to the team they were 12 months ago.

"For me, last season was a difficult year, a difficult season," he added.

"This year, we play from the beginning the style we want and expect to play. We have confidence with the ball and create a lot of chances... I think it's totally different.

"But this is just one game against a fantastic team with an excellent coach in Luis Enrique. They have more maturity [than us]. The last years, they improve together as a team, what they achieve together is amazing."

Flick confirmed that Raphinha, who returned from a hamstring injury as a substitute in the weekend's win at Real Betis, "can start" in Paris, but lamented the team's lack of defenders.

Andreas Christensen, Jules Koundé and Eric García will all miss the game, with Gerard Martín also a minor doubt after picking up a knock against Betis.

Pau Cubarsí, therefore, is the only centre-back guaranteed to be available for the tie, although Flick says he has other options in the squad.

"Rodri can play there, also Frenkie [de Jong] and Álex Campos is with us from the B team," the German coach said.

"I am positive, I hope that everything goes well. It's not the best moment for us, but we have to accept it."

stories.headline: Jasmine Jasudavicius outpoints Erin Blanchfield at UFC Fight Night
stories.summary: Jasmine Jasudavicius stated her case as a contender in the UFC women's featherweight division, dominating Erin Blanchfield on the canvas to win by unanimous decision.
stories.body:
Instability and opportunity permeate the UFC women's flyweight division, which crowned a new champion two weeks ago and has a former two-time champ lurking in the wings while healing from injury. Several other title hopefuls have been jostling to position themselves to go for the gold.

Jasmine Jasudavicius seized the opportunity to make her presence felt among the leading contenders Saturday, dominating Erin Blanchfield on the canvas in a clash of top-10 125-pounders to win by unanimous decision at UFC Fight Night in Edmonton, Alberta.

The fight was the co-main event of a card headlined by Mike Malott's explosive knockout win over Joaquin Buckley. Malott, who like Jasudavicius is from Ontario and had the crowd firmly behind him, landed a knee to the chin that crumbled Buckley, who is No. 8 in the ESPN welterweight rankings and lost his third in a row.

"Hey, guys, I might be soft-spoken," Malott said afterward, "but I'm f---ing hard-hitting."

Malott's knockout came at 2 minutes, 32 seconds of the second round and put a ferocious cap on an event that tied a UFC record with 12 finishes (seven knockouts, five submissions). The other modern-era fight card with a dozen finishes was UFC Fight Night in Belgrade, Serbia, on Aug. 1.

Nevertheless, it was the night's lone bout to go the distance that had the highest stakes. Jasudavicius, No. 8 in the ESPN women's flyweight rankings, pulled off the upset against third-ranked Blanchfield, who came in situated behind only injured former champion Valentina Shevchenko and new titlist Natalia Silva. Blanchfield is also No. 9 in the ESPN women's pound-for-pound top 10.

Jasudavicius (16-4) surely elevated her standing in the 125-pound hierarchy with a robust performance that produced her second straight victory.

Both women came in touted as elite grapplers, and Jasudavicius proved to be a step ahead by repeatedly taking the fight to the ground (five takedowns) and threatening submissions from dominant positions for long stretches of the first two rounds.

"I love grappling," she said. "I understand it. I'm pretty good at it. And I like to show what I've got."

Jasudavicius showed enough to impress the judges, getting the nod on all three scorecards (29-28, 29-28, 29-28). The announcement of the verdict drew a roar from the crowd, which was enthusiastically behind the 37-year-old competing in her home country.

"To be able to fight in Canada, you hear the crowd, man. We're about it," Jasudavicius said.

Jasudavicius and Malott were among a dozen Canadian fighters on the card who went a combined 5-7.

Jasudavicius' victory might not put her in position for an immediate title shot, but she has her sights on a future meeting with the new champion, who defeated her by decision in 2022 in her second UFC fight.

"I want to cross paths with Natalia Silva again," Jasudavicius said. "We had a little bit of history before, so it would be an epic story."

For Blanchfield (14-3), the defeat halted a two-fight winning streak. She outlanded Jasudavicius 62-43 in significant strikes, but the author of five UFC submissions never could get her ground game going. Jasudavicius put Blanchfield on the defensive the whole fight with nearly eight minutes of control time.

stories.headline: NRL transfer whispers: Bulldogs closing in on Skelton return
stories.summary: The NRL season may be over, but the player market is already heating up ahead of November 1. Isaac Issa has news from the Dragons on some key outside backs
stories.body:
The NRL season may be over, but the player market is already heating up ahead of November 1, with clubs beginning to shape their rosters for 2027 and beyond.

From player movement to changes behind the scenes, ESPN NRL Insider Isaac Issa has the latest whispers from around the competition.

Bulldogs closing in on Skelton return

Jeral Skelton is closing in on a return to Canterbury following his departure from the Wests Tigers.

ESPN understands the Bulldogs are in advanced discussions to bring the outside back to the club for the 2027 season.

An agreement is understood to be close, although the deal has yet to be finalised.

Multiple NRL sides eye Knights forward

A Sydney club and a Queensland-based club are monitoring Newcastle forward Mat Croker ahead of November 1.

ESPN understands the two clubs have shown interest in the 27-year-old, who is approaching the final year of his Knights contract and can negotiate with rivals for 2028 onwards from next month.

Rivals keeping tabs on Dragons' Tu

Multiple clubs are monitoring St George Illawarra outside back Setu Tu, with the Dragons yet to begin talks over a contract extension.

Tu is contracted until the end of 2027 and is expected to test the open market from November 1, when rival clubs can negotiate a deal for 2028 and beyond.

The former Warriors outside back joined the Dragons on a development contract this season and is set to move into the club's top 30 squad in 2027.

His ability to cover multiple positions across the backline adds to his appeal as clubs assess their recruitment options.

Rivals monitor Patea as open market looms
Penrith young gun Luron Patea is expected to test the open market from November 1, with multiple clubs keeping tabs on the promising prop.

Patea is contracted until the end of 2027, but the Panthers are yet to begin talks over an extension, leaving rival clubs poised to explore a deal for 2028 and beyond.

Penrith have not granted Patea permission to negotiate with other clubs before November 1.

The Panthers junior made his NRL debut in 2024 and has shown promise during his first-grade opportunities, providing another emerging option in Penrith's forward pack.

He is among several Panthers players approaching the final year of their contracts, with veteran prop Moses Leota also unsigned beyond 2027.

Roosters eye Dockar-Clay reunion
The Roosters have shown interest in a potential return for Zach Dockar-Clay as they explore options to bolster their hooking and utility depth.

ESPN understands the 31-year-old has emerged as an option following his departure from Manly, with discussions remaining at an early stage.

Dockar-Clay spent the 2024 and 2025 seasons with the Roosters before joining the Sea Eagles on a one-year deal for 2026.

Manly confirmed his departure last month after a season in which he claimed the club's NSW Cup best-and-fairest award.

Bostock brushes Dragons links

Dolphins star Jack Bostock has dismissed recent links between himself and the Dragons, admitting this isn't the first time he'd been floated for a club switch.

"I've been linked to a few a clubs," Bostock admitted.

"I don't know about [the Dragons links]."

He said that while he "obviously sees it in the media," his sole focus is the Kangaroos.

Sloan's Dragons stay still a possibility

Tyrell Sloan could yet remain at St George Illawarra next season, with discussions ongoing over a potential stay despite his planned move to Castleford.

There is interest in keeping Sloan at the Dragons, but several hurdles remain before that can become a reality.

Roster space and salary cap room would need to be worked through, while any arrangement would also require Castleford to agree to release him.

Sloan previously admitted he would "love to" remain in the NRL when speaking to Channel Nine in August, after his Castleford deal had been announced.

No agreement has been reached and a stay is far from guaranteed.
